title: The SSD Method and the Algorithmic Economy of Reality: A Universal Interpreter, Latent Twin, and Experimental Test of Deviations from the Born Rule
content: This paper develops an integrated theoretical frameworkunifying three complementary approaches: the Universal Interpreter(UI), the Latent Twin (LT), and the Symbolic Structures of Differences(SSD) method. The central thesis is that reality is not determined byontological necessity but by minimal informational cost---the historythat can be consistently described with the least algorithmic effortenjoys a selection advantage. On this basis, the paper introducesPostulate~P5, which predicts a systematic deviation from the standardBorn rule: the probability of a quantum outcome depends not only on theamplitude but also on the algorithmic complexity of the outcome itself,$P_{\mathrm{UI}}(i) = Z \cdot P_{\mathrm{Born}}(i) \cdot2^{-\lambda \sstar(i)}$,where $\sstar(i)$ is the SSD complexity index and $\lambda > 0$ is aninformational stringency parameter. Section~9 provides a formalmotivation for this step through a decomposition of the Kolmogorovcomplexity of the wave function---without claiming a completederivation, but with precisely stated assumptions. The experimentalframework for testing P5 is based on analyzing the correlation betweenthe empirical frequency of multi-bit quantum measurement outcomes andtheir algorithmic complexity. The SSD index $\sstar$ serves as acomputable proxy for Kolmogorov complexity, complemented byLempel--Ziv and \texttt{zlib} compression for robustness. A pilotsimulation confirms that the proposed statistical test reliablyrecovers an injected parameter $\lambda$ under controlledconditions---but does not confirm that nature follows P5. Empiricalvalidation of the SSD method on numerical sequences, images, and textconfirms its reliability as a measure of global structural complexity,with clearly defined limitations in detecting fine semanticdifferences.
